What is the difference between smoke and sanity testing?

Smoke testing is broad and shallow: run on a new build to decide whether it is stable enough for further testing (app starts, login works, main pages load). Sanity testing is narrow and deep: after a specific bug fix or small change, verify that area works and nothing obvious around it broke. Smoke is often automated and run on every deployment; sanity is often a quick manual check. 💡 Tag a handful of Playwright tests @smoke and run them right after each deploy.
Explain the difference between unit, integration, system and acceptance testing.

Unit tests check one class or method in isolation with dependencies mocked. Integration tests check that components work together — e.g. a Spring service with a real database via Testcontainers. System tests verify the whole deployed application against requirements. Acceptance (UAT) tests are done by business users or the PO to confirm it solves their problem and is ready for release.
What is regression testing and how do you keep it manageable?

Regression testing re-checks existing functionality after a change to make sure nothing that used to work is broken. Keep it manageable by automating stable, high-value paths (unit, API and a small UI suite), running them in CI on every merge, and using risk-based selection for manual regression — focusing on areas touched by the change and critical business flows.
Explain equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis with an example.

For a quantity field accepting 1–100: equivalence partitioning gives three classes — below range (<1), valid (1–100), above range (>100) — plus invalid formats; you test one representative value from each, e.g. -5, 50, 150, abc. Boundary value analysis then tests the edges where off-by-one bugs live: 0, 1, 2 and 99, 100, 101. Together they give high coverage with few cases.
When would you use a decision table?

When the outcome depends on a combination of conditions — e.g. loan approval depends on credit score, income and existing debt. List each condition as a row, every combination as a column (2ⁿ for n boolean conditions, then collapse impossible or equivalent ones), and the expected action for each. It exposes missing or contradictory business rules and maps directly to test cases or a parameterized JUnit test.
What makes a good bug report?

A specific title, environment and build version, preconditions and test data, numbered reproducible steps, expected vs actual result, and evidence such as screenshots, video, console errors, the failing API request/response or a correlation ID. Add severity, priority and frequency (always vs intermittent). One bug per report, factual tone. 💡 If a developer cannot reproduce it from the report alone, the report is not done.
Severity vs priority — give an example of high severity, low priority and the reverse.

Severity is the technical impact; priority is how soon the business wants it fixed. High severity, low priority: the app crashes when exporting a legacy report format almost nobody uses. Low severity, high priority: the company logo or name is wrong on the landing page right before a launch. Severity is usually set by QA, priority by the Product Owner.
Describe the defect life cycle.

A defect is logged as New, triaged and Assigned, worked on (Open/In Progress), marked Fixed and deployed to QA, then Retested. If it passes it is Verified/Closed; if not it is Reopened. Other outcomes are Rejected (works as designed), Duplicate, Deferred to a later release, or Cannot Reproduce.
What is the testing pyramid and why does it matter?

It recommends many fast unit tests, fewer integration/API tests and only a thin layer of UI end-to-end tests. Lower-level tests are faster, cheaper and pinpoint failures; UI tests are slow and more prone to flakiness. Inverting it (the ice-cream cone) leads to slow pipelines and fragile suites. Test each rule at the lowest level that can catch it, and keep E2E for critical user journeys.
Why Playwright over Selenium?

Playwright has built-in auto-waiting and retrying web-first assertions, which removes most explicit waits and flakiness; it supports Chromium, Firefox and WebKit from one API; each test gets an isolated browser context; and it ships with a test runner, parallelism, tracing, video, codegen and network mocking out of the box. Selenium is mature with a huge ecosystem and many language bindings (including Java), but needs more setup and wait handling. Playwright also has Java, Python and .NET bindings.
Which locators do you prefer in Playwright and why?

User-facing locators: getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }), getByLabel, getByText, then getByTestId for elements without accessible names. They mirror how users and assistive tech see the page, so they survive CSS and DOM refactors. Avoid long CSS chains and XPath tied to layout. Locators are strict — if one matches several elements an action throws, which catches ambiguous tests early.
How does auto-waiting work, and how do you handle flaky tests?

Before an action, Playwright waits until the element is attached, visible, stable (not animating), enabled and able to receive events; expect assertions keep retrying until they pass or time out. For flakiness: replace fixed sleeps with web-first assertions, wait on a specific network response with page.waitForResponse if needed, isolate test data so tests do not share state, mock unstable third parties with page.route, and use traces (trace: 'on-first-retry') to find the root cause rather than just adding retries.
What are Playwright fixtures? How do you avoid logging in for every test?

Fixtures provide set-up/tear-down resources to tests by name — built-ins are page, context, browser and request, and you add your own with test.extend (e.g. a page object or a seeded user). To skip repeated logins, create a setup project that logs in once and saves context.storageState({ path: 'auth.json' }), then set use: { storageState: 'auth.json' } for dependent projects.
How do you run Playwright tests in CI?

Install dependencies with npm ci, install browsers with npx playwright install --with-deps (or use the official Playwright Docker image), and run npx playwright test, which is headless by default. In config, enable retries and forbidOnly on CI, use webServer to start the app, and capture screenshots/video/traces on failure. Upload the HTML report as a build artifact and shard large suites across machines.
How do you use environments and variables in Postman?

Define variables like {{baseUrl}}, {{token}} in an environment per target (dev, QA, UAT) and reference them in URLs, headers and bodies, so one collection runs everywhere by switching the environment. Scripts set values dynamically: pm.environment.set('orderId', pm.response.json().id) chains requests. Keep secrets in the current (local) value or a vault, not in exported shared files.
What do you put in Postman pre-request and test scripts?

Pre-request: generate dynamic data (timestamps, UUIDs), compute signatures, or call the auth endpoint with pm.sendRequest and store a bearer token. Tests (post-response): assert status codes, response time, headers, body fields and JSON schema using pm.test and pm.expect, and save values for later requests. 💡 Also test negative cases — 400 for bad input, 401/403 for missing or wrong roles, 404 for unknown IDs.
What is Newman and how is it used in a pipeline?

Newman is Postman's command-line collection runner (installed via npm). In CI after deploying to an environment you run newman run collection.json -e qa.json -r cli,junit --reporter-junit-export results.xml; a failing assertion returns a non-zero exit code and fails the build. You can feed a data file with -d for data-driven iterations. The Postman CLI is a newer alternative that integrates with Postman cloud workspaces.
As a developer, how do you help QA be effective?

Write clear acceptance criteria with QA before development, ship builds with release notes describing what changed and what to retest, provide seed data and per-role test accounts, add data-testid hooks and OpenAPI docs, and log with correlation IDs. When a bug comes in, reproduce it, write a failing test, fix it, and describe the fix and impacted areas in the ticket. Treat QA findings as shared ownership of quality, not criticism.
What is the STLC and what are its phases?

The Software Testing Life Cycle is the structured sequence of testing activities: requirement analysis, test planning, test case design, environment setup, test execution and test closure. Each phase has entry and exit criteria, for example execution starts only when the build passes smoke tests and the environment is ready. In Agile these phases happen inside every sprint rather than once per project.
What goes into a test plan?

Scope and out-of-scope items, test approach (levels, types, what is automated), environments and test data, entry and exit criteria, roles and responsibilities, schedule, risks with mitigations, and deliverables (test cases, reports). A test strategy is the broader, reusable approach; the plan applies it to a specific release.
What is a Requirements Traceability Matrix and why use it?

An RTM maps requirements to test cases and to defects. It proves coverage (no requirement without tests), shows which tests to rerun when a requirement changes, and gives a release-readiness view (which requirements still have open defects). In Jira it is often achieved by linking stories to test cases (Xray, Zephyr) instead of a spreadsheet.
Load vs stress vs soak testing?

Load checks behaviour at expected peak traffic against an SLA. Stress goes beyond capacity to find the breaking point and see whether the system fails gracefully and recovers. Soak holds normal load for a long period to expose leaks, pool exhaustion or gradual slowdowns. 💡 Report percentiles (p95/p99), not averages, because averages hide slow outliers.
What is the Page Object Model and what are its pitfalls?

POM puts locators and user actions for a page in a class, so tests are readable and a UI change is fixed in one place. Pitfalls: giant "god" page objects, putting assertions everywhere inside them, and exposing raw locators instead of meaningful actions. In Playwright, combine POM with fixtures so each test receives ready-made page objects.
How do you do API testing with Playwright instead of Postman?

Use the request fixture or request.newContext({ baseURL, extraHTTPHeaders }) to send GET/POST/PUT/DELETE calls and assert on status() and json(). It lives in the same repo and CI run as the UI tests, shares fixtures and auth state, and is handy for seeding data before a UI test. Postman remains better for exploratory API work and sharing collections with non-developers.
What do you check when testing a REST API?

- Status codes (200/201/204, 400, 401 vs 403, 404, 409, 422, 500).
- Response schema and data types, required fields, and that sensitive fields are not leaked.
- Authentication and authorisation (another user's resource returns 403/404).
- Negative and boundary inputs, validation messages, idempotency of PUT/DELETE, pagination and sorting.
- Headers (Content-Type, CORS, caching) and response time.
How does visual regression testing work, and why is it flaky?

The tool takes a screenshot and compares it pixel by pixel with an approved baseline, failing above a threshold. Flakiness comes from dynamic content, animations, fonts and anti-aliasing that differ between operating systems. Fix it by masking dynamic regions, disabling animations, using a fixed viewport, and creating baselines inside the same Docker image CI uses.
What is contract testing and when is it better than end-to-end tests?

In consumer-driven contract testing (Pact), the consumer's tests produce a contract of the exact requests and responses it needs, and the provider's pipeline verifies against it. It catches breaking API changes early and quickly, without deploying every service together, so it suits microservices and separately deployed front ends. End-to-end tests are still needed for a few critical journeys.
How do you include accessibility in testing?

Automate the basics with axe-core in Playwright or Lighthouse in CI (labels, alt text, contrast, ARIA roles), and do manual checks: keyboard-only navigation, visible focus, logical tab order and a quick screen-reader pass. Target WCAG 2.1/2.2 AA. Using role-based locators like getByRole also nudges the app toward accessible markup.
Verification vs validation?

| Verification | Validation
Question | Are we building the product right? | Are we building the right product?
Checked against | Specifications, designs, standards | Real user needs
Runs code? | Not necessarily: reviews, walkthroughs, static analysis | Yes: testing the working software
Typical activities | Code review, requirement review, unit tests against the spec | System testing, UAT, beta feedback
Rule of thumb: software can pass every verification step and still fail validation, because the specification itself was wrong. You need both.
Black-box vs white-box vs grey-box testing?

| Black-box | White-box | Grey-box
Knowledge of the code | None | Full | Partial: architecture, database, APIs
Tests are based on | Requirements and behaviour | Code paths, branches, conditions | Behaviour, informed by the internals
Techniques | Partitioning, boundary values, decision tables | Statement and branch coverage, path testing | Checking database state after a UI action, API tests
Done by | QA, business users | Developers | QA engineers with technical access
Rule of thumb: unit tests are white-box, UI and acceptance tests are black-box, and most good API and integration testing is grey-box.
Retesting vs regression testing?

| Retesting (confirmation testing) | Regression testing
Purpose | Confirm a specific fixed defect is really fixed | Confirm the change broke nothing else
Scope | The failed test cases only | Areas around the change, or the whole suite
Test cases | Known in advance: the ones that failed | Chosen by risk and impact
Automation | Often manual, steps from the bug report | Ideal for automation, runs in CI
Order | Usually first | After retesting passes
Rule of thumb: retesting looks at the fix, regression testing looks at everything the fix might have touched.
Scripted vs exploratory vs ad hoc testing?

| Scripted | Exploratory | Ad hoc
Preparation | Test cases written in advance | A charter and a time box | None
Design and execution | Separate | At the same time, learning as you go | Unplanned
Documentation | Steps and expected results | Session notes, bugs found | Usually none
Repeatable | Yes | Partly, from the notes | No
Best at | Regression, compliance and audit evidence | Finding unexpected bugs in new features | A quick sanity look
Rule of thumb: automate the scripted checks and spend human time on exploratory sessions; a regulated product such as an EHR still needs the scripted, traceable evidence.
